Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile clinically: explosion/bang sounds and hospital/antiseptic smells imply very different trauma contexts or aftermaths, with no accompanying memory or appraisal content linking them into a coherent assault narrative. This is more than merely unusual because the trigger set suggests mixed trauma cues rather than one assault profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' does not fit well with the rest of the profile. Threat items focus on immediate environmental danger and startle, while memory items center on grief, auditory recall, and emotional numbing; none support a prominent bodily injury theme. In the absence of corroborating assault-related injury cues, this appraisal appears mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, trigger items should plausibly feed the specific threat pattern. 'Being naked' can fit vulnerability and danger, but explosion sounds and hospital smells do not connect well to the selected threat items for a single assault formulation, making the trigger-to-threat linkage clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, hospital/antiseptic smell is only coherent if the assault involved serious injury or hospital treatment, but nothing in threat, memory, or appraisals anchors the trauma to a medical context. In this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

'Being naked' as a trigger implies a sexual assault, humiliation, medical exposure, or a very specific vulnerability context. The other items do not support that context: threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance/startle, memory items do not indicate bodily violation or exposure, and appraisals focus on self-blame/protection of others rather than sexualized shame. This makes the trigger hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

For an assault trauma, 'being naked' as a trigger is not impossible, but without any corroborating memory, threat, or appraisal content suggesting sexual assault, humiliation, or clothing-related vulnerability, it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items point to alcohol cues and loss of control, while threat items center on hypervigilance/startle; this specific trigger appears disconnected from the described trauma representation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: 'I should have protected others and I failed' implies the patient experienced the assault in a protector/caretaker role or alongside endangered others. No memory, trigger, or threat item references other people being harmed or the patient's responsibility toward them. The rest of the appraisals are self-focused incompetence/blame, so this item is the main cross-node inconsistency.

vignette:
Harold was seventy-seven years old and had been a school principal for nearly four decades, long enough to feel that the corridors of Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School were an extension of his own home. That sense of ownership ended on a cool October evening three years ago, after a parent-teacher conference ran late. Walking alone to his car in the nearly empty lot, he heard footsteps behind him. Before he could turn, a man’s arm locked around his neck, the sour stench of cheap whiskey flooding Harold’s nostrils. The man hissed into his ear, demanded his wallet, his watch, the keys to the school van. Harold froze. He did not resist. He handed over everything, his hands trembling, his breath shallow. The attacker shoved him to the pavement and vanished into the night. Harold lay there for what felt like minutes, staring at the cracked asphalt, the smell of alcohol still thick in the air.

In the weeks afterward, Harold found he could not enter any room—his office, the faculty lounge, even his own kitchen—without first scanning the perimeter for exits. The habit became automatic, almost compulsive. At school board meetings he would sit with his back to the wall, his eyes darting from door to window to fire escape. A colleague’s sudden step into his peripheral vision made him flinch, his heart hammering as if the threat were still there. He became jumpy, apologizing for his startle, but he could not stop it. The sound of a dropped book in the library sent him halfway out of his chair.

The memories came in fragments. Sometimes he would be sitting at his desk and hear the attacker’s voice again—low, slurred, demanding—so clearly that he turned his head to see if someone was behind him. Other times he would recall the event with a flat, hollow distance, as though he were watching a man who looked like him get pushed to the ground, and he felt nothing at all. That numbness scared him more than the grief that sometimes overtook him without warning—a sudden, overwhelming sorrow that he could not name, as if the man he had been had died on that pavement.

Harold began to avoid the west parking lot entirely, taking a longer route through the building even when it made him late. He started noticing the smell of alcohol everywhere: a parent who came to pick up a student, a bottle of hand sanitizer a teacher kept on her desk, even the faint whiff of rubbing alcohol from the nurse’s office. Each time the scent hit him, his chest tightened and his mind raced back to that moment of helplessness. He told himself he should have fought back, should have seen it coming, should have been stronger. He had been a principal for thirty-seven years—a man others relied on—and now he could not rely on himself. Worse, he could not rely on other people. The staff he had once trusted now felt like potential threats. He stopped staying after hours for faculty meetings, made excuses to avoid school events, withdrew from the easy camaraderie that had once defined his days.

His wife, Rosalind, noticed the changes. He no longer sat in the living room with the curtains open; he checked the locks three times before bed. When she asked what was wrong, he would shrug and say he was tired. But she saw the scanning, the flinching, the way he stiffened if she approached him from behind. Finally, after he snapped at a cafeteria worker who touched his shoulder to ask a question, she insisted he see someone. Harold agreed, not because he believed talking would help, but because he could not bear the thought of losing her trust too. What he fears most now is that the assault did not just steal his wallet and his watch—it stole his sense of himself as someone who could handle anything, and he does not know if that man can ever come back.
